fetched_contents.text: Recent molecularly imprinted polymers applications in bioanalysis Abstract Molecular imprinted polymers (MIPs) as extraordinary compounds with unique features have presented a wide range of applications and benefits to researchers. In particular when used as a sorbent in sample preparation methods for the analysis of biological samples and complex matrices. Its application in the extraction of medicinal species has attracted much attention and a growing interest. This review focus on articles and research that deals with the application of MIPs in the analysis of components such as biomarkers, drugs, hormones, blockers and inhibitors, especially in biological matrices. The studies based on MIP applications in bioanalysis and the deployment of MIPs in high-throughput settings and optimization of extraction methods are presented. A review of more than 200 articles and research works clearly shows that the superiority of MIP techniques lies in high accuracy, reproducibility, sensitivity, speed and cost effectiveness which make them suitable for clinical usage. Furthermore, this review present MIP-based extraction techniques and MIP-biosensors which are categorized on their classes based on common properties of target components. Extraction methods, studied sample matrices, target analytes, analytical techniques and their results for each study are described. Investigations indicate satisfactory results using MIP-based bioanalysis. According to the increasing number of studies on method development over the last decade, the use of MIPs in bioanalysis is growing and will further expand the scope of MIP applications for less studied samples and analytes. Keywords: Molecular imprinted polymers, Bioanalysis, Extraction techniques, Biological samples Introduction Molecular imprinted polymers (MIPs) have been in focus due to their special properties in many fields during the last decade. Many optimizations and developments of MIP techniques have been achieved for a range of goals. The most common applications of MIPs are detecting and quantifying of special targets in the field of chemistry. Due to the importance of analyzing drugs, biomarkers and other analytes in biological samples, scientists have developed MIP-based techniques to make analysis procedures more selective, sensitive, rapid and cost-effective. These efforts will allow MIP-based extraction techniques to be used as common approaches for clinical usage. According to BelBruno (2019), for the first time the phrase “imprinted polymer” has been reported by Andersson et al. (1984). However, Wulff (2013) has claimed that the molecularly imprinted synthetic polymers were discovered in 1972 in his laboratory and his first article related to imprinted polymers is published in 1985 (Wulff et al. 1985). For more details, Wulff, in his early researches, has applied imprinted polymers in catalytic reactions (Liu and Wulff 2004; Wulff et al. 2006; Wulff and Knorr 2001; Wulff and Liu 2012) like K. Shea as well, who has reported on rather unique biological applications, like a plastic antibody inserted into living mice (BelBruno 2019). By the way, the presence of numerous MIP approaches and the obvious attention paid to these techniques is the consequence of these early researchers’ evaluations. Several methods are recommended for the preparation of MIPs, some of which include synthesis, phase inversion and soft lithography or surface stamping methods. The synthesis methods are the most popular technique among researchers. In such methods, functional monomers interact with target molecules for developing a network of covalently or non-covalently complexes. Pyrrole, methacrylic acid (MAA), aniline, methyl methacrylate (MMA) and acrylamide are some of the most common functional monomers (Fig. 1) (BelBruno 2019; Xu et al. 2020). Briefly, in a synthesis method, the component process mainly includes a porogen solvent, a cross linker, a functional monomer, an initiator and a template as shown in Fig. 2. Each component in a synthesis process plays significant roles in which changing and improving one of items will lead to optimized MIPs as a result. For instance, choosing a good template for a special analyte is very determinative in sensitivity and selectivity of the extraction process, or finding the best way for removing templates and analytes (washing and eluting) in the last step is extremely important because an unsuccessful removal may affects the final results(BelBruno 2019). Polymerization is the first crucial level in MIP formation which monomers, initiators, cross-linkers and even every polymerization method impact on results. Hence, polymerization methodologies and the optimal components for each analyte in different matrices must be investigated in order to obtain acceptable modifications(Souza et al. 2016; Asiabi et al. 2016; McKitterick et al. 2020a; Pajewska-Szmyt et al. 2020; Sartore et al. 2020; Gama and Bottoli 2017). Nanomaterials as sorbents are extensively applied in various extraction methods. Based on extensive researches, various nanomaterials are introduced and utilized in many extraction techniques. Among all nanomaterial sorbents, MIP nanoparticles have gained much attention of researches to have prosperous usage in significant extraction techniques (Ahmadi et al. 2017). Some examples of utilizing these sorbents are presented in this review. Finally, synthesized polymers may have a good selectivity on target molecules in the reason of binding supplementary sites with template in shape, size and also in the position of the functional groups (He et al. 2007; Djozan et al. 2011, 2012; Song et al. 2014; Sellergren et al. 1988; Rachkov and Minoura 2000). MIP nanoparticles have been thoroughly reviewed by Fresco-Cala et al. (2020). MIPs are good candidates for the selective detection of Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary psychoactive ingredient in Cannabis, as there is an emergent need for new technologies to selectively detect and monitor THC for health, safety, and quality control applications, especially portable miniaturized devices (e.g. for roadside tests). Microfluidic gas sensors are modifiable miniaturized devices that selectively detect a target gas through microchannel modifications. In this study, highly selective microfluidic gas sensors toward THC are reported based on MIP coatings. The sensors' performance was evaluated by exposure to THC, Cannabidiol (CBD), methanol, and ethanol samples. Molecularly imprinted polymers (MIPs) are highly cross-linked polymers that can recognize and capture target compounds sterically and electrostatically. Solid-phase extraction (SPE) methods using MIP as adsorbents have been widely developed for selective extraction of target analytes. In this study, we evaluated the extraction efficacy of the following 10 cannabis-related compounds in human urine and plasma samples using a commercially available MIP-SPE cartridge: Δ⁹-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), Δ⁸-THC, tetrahydrocannabivarin, cannabigerol, cannabichromene, cannabidiol, cannabinol, 11-nor-9-carboxy-Δ⁹-THC, 11-nor-9-carboxy-Δ⁸-THC, and 11-hybroxy-Δ⁹-THC. The recovery rates were 49–102 % for urine and 34–87 % for plasma, and matrix effects were 49–91 % for urine and 45–108 % for plasma. The proposed method is expected to be applicable for the extraction and quantification of cannabinoids and their metabolites in actual human biological samples. MIPs for THC and metabolite recognition are synthesized around a template molecule that closely resembles the target analyte, with THC and its metabolites used as the imprinting templates in multiple sources. The evidence indicates that studies explicitly target Δ9-THC and THC-COOH as the template molecules, and one review also notes the use of Δ9-THC and THC-COOH in template–reagent interaction assessments [N1-R1][N1-R2]. In a primary MIP application, a cannabinoid-specific MIP was synthesized using Δ9-THC-COOH as the template molecule, while other sources describe MIPs targeting cannabinoids such as THC, CBD, and metabolites including THC-COOH and related compounds in biological matrices [N5-F2][N5-F3].

The structure of the template is critical to imprinting, because the polymer is designed to form a recognition site that matches the target analyte’s shape, size, and functional-group positions. The review explicitly states that MIPs are designed to selectively bind target analytes through steric and electrostatic recognition, and that the binding sites are formed by the template and functional monomer interaction during synthesis [N5-F1]. A primary MIP study also states that the prepared MIP is highly selective for cannabinoids typically found in blood and urine, and for cannabinol (CBN) and cannabidiol (CBD), reinforcing that the recognition is not limited to THC alone but extends to related cannabis biomarkers [N5-F3].

For functional monomers, the evidence points to common choices such as methacrylic acid (MAA), acrylamide, methyl methacrylate (MMA), and aniline, and more specifically, ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA) is explicitly used as a functional monomer in a primary MIP study for cannabinoids [N5-F1][N5-F3]. Crosslinkers are also central to polymer stability and selectivity; one source identifies divinylbenzene (DVB) as a crosslinker used in a cannabinoid MIP, while another review notes that crosslinkers, along with functional monomers, initiators, and porogen solvents, are key components of the synthesis process [N5-F2][N5-F1]. The review also emphasizes that each synthesis component plays a significant role, and changing one can optimize the final MIP [N5-F1].

Synthesis protocols generally follow a common sequence: template and functional monomer complex formation, crosslinker incorporation, polymerization, and then template removal. The review describes polymerization as the first crucial step, and it states that functional monomers interact with target molecules to develop a network of covalently or non-covalently complexes [N5-F1]. A primary study reports that the MIP was synthesized using a functional monomer, crosslinker, and initiator, with the template removed after polymerization [N5-F3]. Another source gives a mole ratio of 1:4:20 for metabolite template: functional monomer: cross-linking agent, suggesting that precise stoichiometry is used to allow successful imprinting [N1-R5]. Template removal is explicitly noted as a critical step because incomplete removal can affect final results [N5-F1].

Overall, MIP synthesis for THC/metabolite recognition combines a carefully chosen template, functional monomer, crosslinker, and polymerization conditions, with the aim of creating a selective binding site that can later be used for extraction or detection [N1-R1][N1-R5][N5-F1][N5-F2][N5-F3].

MIP-based assays have several advantages over conventional immunoassays, but they also face common failure points and practical limitations. One major advantage is batch-to-batch consistency and ease of mass production, which the evidence states is a key benefit of MIPs compared to biological materials such as monoclonal antibodies [N2-R1]. The review also notes that MIPs are used in biosensors and extraction methods and can be tailored for high accuracy, reproducibility, sensitivity, speed, and cost-effectiveness [N5-F1]. In addition, MIPs are attractive because they can be designed to recognize targets through steric and electrostatic interactions, which can improve selectivity for complex matrices [N5-F1].

Common failure points include incomplete template removal, variability in polymerization conditions, and matrix effects. The review explicitly says that changing one synthesis component can lead to optimized MIPs, but that incomplete removal of template and analytes after washing and eluting can affect final results [N5-F1]. Another source emphasizes that conventional immunoassays with colorimetric or fluorimetric detection generally display favorable detection limits but must be reconfigured for different applications [N4-R3]. The evidence also indicates that detection limits vary widely across methods, with absorbance reaching 10⁻⁸ to 10⁻⁷ M and fluorescence reaching 10⁻¹⁰ to 10⁻¹³ M, showing that sensitivity can differ substantially depending on the detection approach [N4-R4].

Validation requirements are therefore important for MIP-based assays. The review stresses that MIP techniques must be validated for accuracy, reproducibility, sensitivity, and practical applicability, and that validation is especially important when comparing MIPs with conventional methods [N5-F1]. The same primary study reports linearity, precision, accuracy, recovery, and matrix effects as validation parameters, including correlation coefficients > 0.994 for urine and > 0.999 for plasma, and satisfactory precision and accuracy [N5-F3]. A general review on illicit-drug detection notes that biosensors present a clear trade-off between analytical performance and practical applicability, reinforcing that validation is necessary to balance sensitivity with usability [N2-R1].

Practical issues include storage, reuse, and matrix effects. The evidence suggests that MIPs are generally reusable, but storage conditions and long-term stability are not explicitly detailed here. What is clear is that matrix effects can be substantial; one urine study reports matrix effects of 49–91% for urine and 45–108% for plasma, indicating that urine is a complex matrix that can significantly influence analyte behavior [N5-F3]. Another primary MIP study reports that the method is stable for 72 hours in the autosampler and that dilution and matrix effects must be controlled [N5-F3]. Taken together, MIP-based assays are promising but require careful optimization, validation, and matrix correction to achieve reliable results in urine testing [N2-R1][N4-R4][N5-F1][N5-F3].

### 1) MIP synthesis for THC and metabolite recognition

MIP synthesis starts with a template molecule, functional monomers, crosslinkers, and polymerization conditions. The evidence emphasizes that functional monomers interact with the target molecule to form a network of covalently or non-covalently bound complexes, while crosslinkers stabilize the structure [N5-F1]. MIP-based assays for THC and metabolites in urine are judged by selectivity, detection sensitivity, and analytical performance. MIP-based assays have several advantages over conventional immunoassays. This means MIPs are not limited to THC alone but are also used for a broad range of cannabis biomarkers, including metabolites and related cannabinoids.

### 1) MIP synthesis for THC and metabolite recognition

MIP synthesis starts with a template molecule, functional monomers, crosslinkers, and polymerization conditions. The evidence emphasizes that functional monomers interact with the target molecule to form a network of covalently or non-covalently bound complexes, while crosslinkers stabilize the structure [N5-F1]. Common functional monomers mentioned in the branch reports include methacrylic acid (MAA), acrylamide, methyl methacrylate (MMA), and aniline; one primary study explicitly reports ethylene glycol dimethacrylate (EGDMA) as the functional monomer [N5-F1][N5-F3]. Crosslinkers are also central; one source identifies divinylbenzene (DVB) as a crosslinker in a cannabinoid MIP, and another review notes that crosslinkers, along with functional monomers, initiators, and porogen solvents, are key components of the synthesis process [N5-F2][N5-F1].

A common mole ratio of 1:4:20 is cited for metabolite template: functional monomer: cross-linking agent, suggesting that precise stoichiometry is used to allow successful imprinting [N1-R5]. Polymerization is the first crucial step in MIP formation, and the review emphasizes that changing any synthesis component can affect the final MIP, with incomplete template removal after washing and eluting being a critical failure point [N5-F1]. The synthesis sequence therefore generally follows template-complex formation, crosslinker incorporation, polymerization, and then template removal [N5-F1][N5-F3].

### 2) MIP-based detection and binding formats for urine testing

MIPs are used in urine testing as selective sorbents or coatings in binding assays. For urine testing, sample preparation is a major upstream step. The branch reports indicate that SPE is the dominant extraction method, with evidence from general urine-extraction sources supporting the use of SPE and comparisons with liquid-liquid extraction [N3-R1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. A primary MIP study reports a commercially available MIP-SPE cartridge for cannabis-related compounds in human urine and plasma, and another study uses a cone-shaped device with a polypropylene membrane for microsolid-phase extraction (μ-SPE) in batch mode [N5-F3][N5-F2]. ### 3) Selectivity, detection limits, and performance in urine

MIP-based assays for THC and metabolites in urine are judged by selectivity, detection sensitivity, and analytical performance. A primary study reports detection sensitivities from sub-ng/mL to ng/mL levels, with good linearity of calibration curves and satisfactory precision and accuracy [N5-F3]. Selectivity is also evident in the reported performance. The review notes that MIPs are designed to selectively bind target analytes through steric and electrostatic recognition [N5-F1]. A primary MIP study reports that the prepared MIP is highly selective for cannabinoids typically found in blood and urine, and also for cannabinol (CBN) and cannabidiol (CBD) [N5-F3]. ### 4) Practical applications in urine analysis

In urine analysis, cannabis biomarker-specific MIPs are commonly targeted toward THC and its major metabolites, especially Δ9-THC-COOH and related compounds. ### 5) Strengths, limitations, and practical considerations

MIP-based assays have several advantages over conventional immunoassays. One major advantage is batch-to-batch consistency and ease of mass production, which the evidence states is a key benefit of MIPs compared to biological materials such as monoclonal antibodies [N2-R1]. The review also notes that MIPs are used in biosensors and extraction methods and can be tailored for high accuracy, reproducibility, sensitivity, speed, and cost-effectiveness [N5-F1].
